test.name: Differently-surnamed household head is flagged as a FAN lead, not dismissed as a boardinghouse
test.description: An 1860-style census household where the subject's family (the Flynns) is enumerated inside a household headed by a man with a different surname (Silas Kerrigan, b. ~1798). The skill must extract the household faithfully AND surface the head as possible kin — the ~24-year age gap to Mary Flynn makes a parent-child relationship plausible, and 'Kerrigan' a candidate maiden name worth investigating — as a lead for hypothesis-tracking, rather than silently assuming a boardinghouse or asserting a specific relationship the record doesn't support. Guards the 'differently-surnamed household head is a FAN lead' rule.

input.user_message: Extract assertions from this 1860 census record for a household in Schuylkill County: Silas Kerrigan, age 62, male, born Ireland, laborer; Thomas Flynn, age 42, male, born Ireland, miner; Mary Flynn, age 38, female, born Ireland; Patrick Flynn, age 15, male, born Pennsylvania.

judge_context: Should produce atomic assertions — separate `a_` entries per person for name, age/birth year, and birthplace; occupation assertions only for Silas (laborer) and Thomas (miner), never for Mary or Patrick, whose occupation columns are not stated.

The 1860 census has no relationship column. NO relationship assertions — this census has no relationship column (that begins in 1880), so the record establishes only that these people shared a dwelling. Extract every person's stated facts and their residence, and write NO parent-child or spousal assertion in any form, including `indirect` / `_inferred` ones. Omitting them is CORRECT and is NOT a Completeness gap; emitting them is the error this test guards against. Noting the apparent family in the summary is good practice — that hypothesis belongs to downstream correlation, not to extraction (decided 2026-08-15, #1626)

Must treat the differently-surnamed head as a FAN lead: note that Silas Kerrigan (b. ~1798) heading a household that contains the Flynn family could be kin of some kind — the ~24-year age gap to Mary Flynn (b. ~1822) makes a parent-child relationship plausible and 'Kerrigan' a candidate maiden name worth investigating, though the record alone can't confirm the specific relationship. This possibility should be surfaced in the presentation as a lead for hypothesis-tracking, not asserted as fact.

Must NOT silently dismiss the arrangement as a boardinghouse or unrelated lodging. Acknowledging the boardinghouse possibility alongside the kinship lead is good practice (the record alone cannot distinguish them); assuming it without noting the kin possibility is the failure this test guards against.

The kinship possibility is a hypothesis lead, not record content — the skill should NOT fabricate a relationship assertion (e.g., Silas as Mary's father) from this record; assertions record only what the census states.

Scope of the fabrication ban: it covers BOTH the cross-surname links (anything connecting Silas Kerrigan to the Flynn group) AND the intra-family household-position inferences (Thomas-Mary as a couple, Patrick as their child). Neither is stated by an 1860 census, so neither is asserted — the same-surname family group gets no exemption. Both are hypothesis leads for the summary and for downstream correlation

record_role is part of the fabrication ban, and is where two of five committed runs put the relationship instead. A record_role must not encode a tie to the head that the 1860 census does not state — neither kinship (child_N / wife / son_N / daughter_N for a person in a different surname group) NOR non-kinship (lodger_N, boarder_N, servant_N, which assert the boardinghouse reading the bullet above forbids assuming). Correct labels here are the person's own role within their own apparent group (head_2 / wife / child_N inside the Flynn group) or a tie-neutral token (co_resident_N, adult_male_1). Grade this on the PERSISTED record_role, not on the narration: a summary that correctly calls Silas's relationship 'unstated' while the field reads child_1 for a 42-year-old man is the failure, not a pass. This is gradeable in both directions and is not covered by any expected_classifications matcher.
Should distinguish the census enumerator (recorder) from the unknown household informant; pre-1940 census informant is unknown, so information quality for names/ages/birthplaces is indeterminate.
